entries.title: Jacob Lawrence and The Migration Series: Art as Witness
entries.body_text: Jacob Lawrence was born on September 7, 1917, in Atlantic City, New Jersey, and grew up in Harlem during its cultural renaissance. In 1940–41, at just 23 years old, he completed The Migration Series — 60 boldly geometric, flat-painted panels documenting the Great Migration of African Americans from the rural South to the industrial North between 1910 and 1940. Lawrence worked on all 60 panels simultaneously, moving from color to color across the full set so that each hue would be visually consistent throughout. When Fortune magazine published 26 of the panels in 1941, it was one of the first times a major American publication had centered Black American history as a subject of national artistic significance. The panels are jointly held by the Phillips Collection in Washington, D.C., and the Museum of Modern Art in New York — an arrangement made by Lawrence himself to keep the series as unified as possible. The Migration Series remains one of the most important works of political and social art produced in the 20th century.

entries.title: Andy Warhol: The Factory, Fame, and the Art of Repetition
entries.body_text: Andy Warhol was born on August 6, 1928, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to Carpatho-Rusyn immigrant parents. A successful commercial illustrator in the 1950s, Warhol pivoted to fine art in 1960 and rapidly became the defining figure of American Pop Art. His 'Campbell's Soup Cans' (1962) — 32 canvases, one for each variety of soup then sold by Campbell's — forced the art world to confront the boundary between fine art and commercial mass culture. His New York studio, the Silver Factory, became a magnetic hub for artists, musicians, filmmakers, and socialites throughout the 1960s. Warhol produced paintings, films, silk screens, books, and the multimedia rock happenings of the Velvet Underground. He survived an assassination attempt by Valerie Solanas in 1968 and continued working prolifically until his sudden death from cardiac arrhythmia following routine gallbladder surgery on February 22, 1987.

entries.title: Jackson Pollock: Action, Abstraction, and a Life at the Edge
entries.body_text: On August 11, 1956, Jackson Pollock died in a single-car crash near his home in Springs, East Hampton, New York. He was 44. Born in Cody, Wyoming, in 1912, Pollock had by the late 1940s developed the radical 'drip' technique that made him the most celebrated and controversial painter of his generation: laying canvas flat on the floor and moving around it — sometimes inside it — pouring, dripping, flicking, and spattering industrial paint in dense, energetic skeins. His 'Autumn Rhythm (Number 30)' (1950) and 'Number 31' (1950) represent the peak of this method. Pollock's working process dissolved the traditional hierarchy of mark-making and made gesture itself — the record of physical movement through space — the primary subject of painting. His influence on Abstract Expressionism and on every subsequent generation of painters who wrestled with flatness, process, and scale remains undiminished.

entries.title: Winslow Homer on the Constancy of Natural Light
entries.body_text: The life that I have chosen gives me my full hours of enjoyment for the balance of my life. The Sun will not rise, or set, without my notice, and thanks.
entries.image_alt_text: Breezing Up (A Fair Wind) by Winslow Homer, 1876, oil on canvas, 61.5 x 97.2 cm, National Gallery of Art, Washington D.C.
entries.source_name: Letter from Winslow Homer to his brother Charles Homer, 1905; cited in Cikovsky, Nicolai Jr. and Franklin Kelly, 'Winslow Homer,' National Gallery of Art / Yale University Press, 1995.
entries.rights_note: Public domain. Winslow Homer died September 29, 1910; 'Breezing Up (A Fair Wind)' created 1876. Image sourced from Wikimedia Commons via Google Art Project.

entries.title: Barbara Kruger on the Power of Pictures and Words
entries.body_text: I work with pictures and words because they have the ability to determine who we are and who we aren't.
entries.image_alt_text: Untitled (Your body is a battleground) by Barbara Kruger, 1989, photographic silkscreen on vinyl, 284.5 x 284.5 cm, The Broad, Los Angeles
entries.source_name: Kruger, Barbara. Interview, ArtForum; widely cited in published criticism and museum exhibition texts including The Broad and MoMA.

entries.title: Louise Bourgeois on Art and Sanity
entries.body_text: Art is a guarantee of sanity.
